The Boston Red Sox have a decision to make with outfielder Jarren Duran this offseason.
If you're a Red Sox fan who has been following the club over the last few years, or simply a baseball fan in general who has followed trade rumors, you've likely seen Duran's name a lot. His name was out there as a trade candidate before the 2025 season, ahead of the 2025 trade deadline, before the 2026 season and before the 2026 trade deadline. In every scenario, the Red Sox kept the speedster.
The offseason is now here for Boston and there surely will be trade chatter again with the Red Sox still having a surplus of talented outfielders. Plus, Duran just had the worst offensive season of his career to this point at the same time. The 30-year-old has two more seasons of team control beyond the 2026 season and arbitration is going to play a big role this offseason in the decision-making process. On Friday, MLB Trade Rumors released its salary estimates for arbitration-eligible players and had Duran at $11.1 million. When it comes to projecting arbitration salaries, MLB Trade Rumors is considered to be among the very best in the business.
What Should Boston Do?
Now, of course, nothing is guaranteed at this exact moment about that $11.1 million number. But if that's the direction Duran's contract is going to go, it's going to make a decision more difficult this winter. In 2026, Duran made $7.7 million and batted .207 with a .266 on-base percentage. Now, of course, his 20 homers, 69 RBIs and 21 stolen bases were good. But those batting average and on-base percentage numbers are almost unplayable.
There's no denying Duran's talent. When he's at his best, he's a five-tool player. But the 2026 season wasn't his best. In 2024, he was a 9.0 WAR player. In 2025, he was a 4.9 WAR player in what was viewed as a somewhat down year. In 2026, he was a 0.4 WAR player. It's going to be hard to argue for the increase to a number in the range that MLB Trade Rumors projected with two straight years of regression. Plus, now Duran is 30 years old.
The deadline to tender contracts is the last Friday before Thanksgiving each November. This year, that day falls on Nov. 20. If the Red Sox non-tender Duran, he would simply enter free agency. If the Red Sox tender him a contract, then that's when this number — or something similar — will come into play. For a club that needs to add more power, shelling out that much cash to Duran would be a lot. Also, a price tag that high could be difficult to trade after he just had a difficult season.
When it comes to Duran, the first decision that's going to come is tendering — or non-tendering — him. If they were to non-tender him, they save the cash but get nothing in return. It's a difficult call, to say the least.

The Boston Red Sox and Jarren Duran have been involved in swirling trade rumors for a while now.
Essentially all of last offseason was spent with the premise that the Red Sox had too many outfielders and that one was bound to get traded.
That never came to fruition, though, and so Duran remained in Boston for the 2026 season.
He struggled mightily, batting just .207 with limited power, and so questions will arise again.
The Red Sox still have the same amount of outfielders. Duran might not be worth as much, but he also might not be as crucial for Boston to keep around.
A year later, could a trade materialize?
That’s one question being asked as the Red Sox enter their offseason after being swept in two games in the AL Wild Card Series by the rival New York Yankees.
There are big questions for the sport of baseball to answer as a whole this winter. In Boston, though, Duran is going to be one of the biggest things to solve, one way or another.
Jarren Duran Trade Plans
ESPN’s David Schoenfield wrote about this question almost immediately following the Red Sox season ending, and he seems to arrive at the conclusion that a trade could definitely be coming.
“That leaves trading Duran on the agenda,” Schoenfield writes. “Roman Anthony’s nearly four-month stint on the IL meant the four-outfielders-for-three-positions problem never actually turned into a problem, but after hitting just .207/.266/.361, Duran is clearly fourth on the depth chart. His trade value took a nosedive, but he still somehow has two years left of team control, and the Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.”
There is certainly value for an acquiring team in the fact that Duran still has two more years under contract. Especially considering what a shortened season might do to player value, a team knowing it would also have Duran for 2028 could be appealing to anyone who still believes in his talent.
There may not be a lot of suitors, but Schoenfield writes that the “Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.” It’ll just be up to Boston at that point to follow through on the deal.
Why Red Sox Offseason Might Be Slow Otherwise
Aside from Duran, Schoenfield doesn’t think Boston will be very busy. They’ve already taken care of a bunch of things.
“While the Red Sox had a revolving door at shortstop and second base in 2026 — six different players started at short and seven at second — those positions will probably be resolved in 2027 with top prospect Franklin Arias and Curtis Mead, the trade deadline acquisition the Red Sox were going to play at second base until he got injured his first game with the team,” Schoenfield writes. “Trevor Story still has one more year left on his contract, but there’s no reason he should be playing ahead of Arias next season.”
Schoenfield also references the recent trades for Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Erik Miller as limiting the need for moves, since those guys all are under contract still.
His only other question: Does Sonny Gray retire, or return, or neither? The Red Sox still have things to figure out, just maybe not as much as some years.

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox fans entered Game 1 of the Wild Card Series on Tuesday night with cautious optimism. They hoped to avenge last year's crushing loss against Massachusetts native Cam Schlittler by beating him up this time around, with their ace, Payton Tolle, on the mound, and their star outfielder, Roman Anthony, in the leadoff spot.
Well, Tolle was fine, but Schlittler was dominant, the New York Yankees won convincingly, and, as if that wasn't bad enough, Anthony left the game in the sixth inning for a pinch-hitter. So to sum up, the Red Sox are down in this best-of-three series one game to none, and could be without their young star with their season on the line on Wednesday. Not great!
Roman Anthony injury update brings worst case of deja vu to Red Sox fans
Anthony missed more than three months on the Injured List with a right wrist injury. The Red Sox were able to rebound following an atrocious start without him, somehow, but obviously missed him dearly when he was out. Sure enough, the injury Anthony suffered on Tuesday was an aggravation of the ailment that kept him out for roughly half the year, according to manager Chad Tracy.
When asked whether Anthony will play on Wednesday, all he said was, "We'll have to see what tomorrow brings." That does not sound encouraging for a Red Sox team whose season is officially on the line.
As frustrating as this injury is, it's a bit less shocking that it occurred, knowing that he appeared to have tweaked it on an awkward swing in Sunday's game. What's particularly irritating is that Sunday's game was completely meaningless for both Boston and the Cubs, their opponent. Anthony did not have to play, but did, and might've ended his season in the process.
He might play, but Anthony struck out in each of his first two at-bats of Tuesday's game, and who knows if he's close to healthy. This is not good news for Boston, and neither is their projected lineup for Game 2 without him.
Projected Red Sox lineup without Roman Anthony shows they're in trouble
| Player | Position |
|---|---|
| 1. Jahmai Jones | DH |
| 2. Adley Rutschman | C |
| 3. Willson Contreras | 1B |
| 4. Wilyer Abreu | RF |
| 5. Ceddanne Rafaela | CF |
| 6. Nick Sogard | 2B |
| 7. Trevor Story | SS |
| 8. Caleb Durbin | 3B |
| 9. Jarren Duran | LF |
There's some talent here. Jahmai Jones has crushed left-handed pitching since arriving with the Red Sox, so perhaps he can set the tone in Anthony's place against left-hander Max Fried on Wednesday. Guys like Adley Rutschman, Willson Contreras, Wilyer Abreu and even Ceddanne Rafaela are capable of doing damage at all times. Hey, even Trevor Story doubled on Tuesday for Boston's only extra-base hit.
With that being said, though, the Red Sox looked rather punchless at the plate all of Tuesday's game. I know Schlittler started it, but one extra-base hit in a playoff game is pretty pathetic. That was with Anthony playing in half the contest. Can the Red Sox score runs against Fried, who is also elite, by the way, without Anthony? It's hard to believe that, especially with how this offense has looked in September.
Red Sox season feels finished after Game 1 gut punch
It'd be foolish to count out any postseason team, especially one like the Red Sox, who went on a 32-5 run this season. They've proven they can bounce back from adversity, and if they can just find a way to win Game 2, suddenly they'd be one win away from eliminating the Yankees and advancing to the ALDS.
Still, only one team has won Game 1 of a Wild Card Series and gone on to lose that best-of-three affair since MLB made the permanent switch to that format in 2022. That team? The Boston Red Sox, who blew a 1-0 series lead to these Yankees in the Bronx. The circumstances were different, though. The Yankees were the home team, they still had Aaron Judge healthy, and they didn't lose 9-0 the night before.
I don't want to count Boston out, but even getting to Game 3 has been challenging for teams that drop Game 1 of the Wild Card series. The Red Sox have their work cut out for them, especially if Anthony has to miss time and/or is at all compromised due to his wrist injury, which, at this point, feels likely.

The Red Sox paid a handsome price for former Orioles catcher Adley Rutschman at the MLB trade deadline, dealing a handful of top prospects for the former No. 1 overall pick. After a middling second half, Chad Tracy’s first playoff lineup decision as manager of the Red Sox puts a lot of faith in Rutschman.
Tracy unveiled the Red Sox starting lineup that would hit against Yankees ace and likely Cy Young Cam Schlittler in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card at Yankee Stadium. Unsurprisingly, former top overall prospect in baseball Roman Anthony is leading off, but it’s Rutschman batting second ahead of All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras in the #3 spot.
Rutschman’s place in the order had been messed around with in the final days of the regular season, with Rutschman batting second, third or fifth on a given night. Much of Rutschman’s batting second has to do with the loss of Mickey Gasper to a biceps injury, as Gasper was usually the guy Tracy wanted on base ahead of the Red Sox’ power bats.
Chad Tracy’s Informed Adley Rutschman Lineup Decision
The decision to bat Rutschman second isn’t arbitrary: Rutschman is one of just two Red Sox players currently to have an extra base hit against Schlittler this year, along with third baseman Caleb Durbin, who hit a two-run home run against him earlier this season.
The Red Sox’ starting nine of Anthony, Rutschman, Contreras, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Nick Sogard, Jarren Duran, Trevor Story and Durbin is just a combined 8-for-59 (.136) with the two extra base hits against Schlittler this season.
The lineup appears to be Chad Tracy’s best attempt at getting some runs across against Schlittler. The announcement comes amid musings that the Red Sox reportedly “wore out” the Rays’ Trajekt machine mimicking Schlittler’s arsenal this weekend while they were playing their season finale against the Cubs in the domed Tropicana Field due to heavy rain in Boston.
AL Wild Card Preview
The Yankees put out a platoon-heavy lineup of their own, starting veterans Paul Goldschmidt and Amed Rosario over Luis Garcia Jr. at first and Jazz Chisholm Jr at second. The Yankees got a “mini break” as their games against the Orioles on Saturday and Sunday, with no clinching scenarios on the line, were canceled due to the same nor’easter that pushed the Sox and Cubs to Florida.
It’ll be a rematch of the 2025 American League Wild Card series, which the Yankees won in three electrifying games, but with a different cast of characters, Rutschman chief among them. The Red Sox will surely rely on him finding his bat this series after posting a disappointing .222/.278/.410 slash in the final two months of the season after the trade from Baltimore. He’ll be thrown immediately into the fire against Schlittler, and it should certainly be a fun one.

The Boston Red Sox will be taking on the New York Yankees in the American League wild-card round this year, which is a rematch from last season.
Boston was able to clinch a spot in the postseason following an impressive run during the middle of the year to get back into the race. But the Red Sox couldn’t do enough to overtake the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East, and now they will be entering a three-game series that will determine their fate.
The longtime rivals are gearing up for Game 1 of the highly anticipated series, with each trying to make a statement against the other. New York won the season series 7-6, but the entire matchup was extremely close, leading to the thought that this playoff matchup will be as well.
Last season, the Yankees defeated the Red Sox in three games to move on to the ALDS. Boston will be looking for some revenge here, and the series is again being played in New York.
Jarren Duran Decision Made by Red Sox
Ahead of Game 1, the Red Sox have now released the lineup that they will use against the Yankees. Within the lineup, outfielder Jarren Duran will be hitting seventh for Boston today.
Duran will be playing in left field.
Red Sox 9/29
R. Anthony DH
A. Rutschman C
W. Contreras 1B
W. Abreu RF
C. Rafaela CF
N. Sogard 2B
J. Duran LF
T. Story SS
C. Durbin 3B
P. Tolle SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 29, 2026
Duran has seen a tough season at the plate take place, and it’s hurt the overall ceiling of this Red Sox team. Overall, the former All-Star has hit .207 with 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, and 21 stolen bases, while posting an OPS of .627.
Boston has been waiting for Duran to break out of his slump all season long, but to this point, nothing has worked. But if he can get his bat going in the playoffs, his struggles from the regular season will be forgiven.
Can Red Sox Take Down Yankees?
For the Red Sox to win this series, guys like Duran are going to need to step up heavily. New York will be without star Aaron Judge due to injury, and the Red Sox need to take advantage of this fact.
Boston’s pitching staff will be counted on heavily in this series as they try to match the strong starting rotation from the Yankees. But luckily for the Red Sox, the team will be getting back ace left-hander Garrett Crochet from injury.
It has been a long time coming for Crochet, with him last pitching on April 25 for this team. Crochet has been trying to come back all year, but the Red Sox finally saw progress over the last few weeks, and he has been added to the playoff roster.
If Crochet can make an impact as a relief pitcher, it could go a long way for this team against the Yankees. Boston is behind the eight ball when it comes to the pitching in the series, and Crochet gives them at least a fighting chance.
The Red Sox and Yankees will kick off the opening game of the series at 5:00 p.m. PT/8:00 p.m. ET from Yankee Stadium.

Apple vs. Microsoft. Coke vs. Pepsi. Marvel vs. DC. Ford vs. General Motors.
All child’s play compared to Yankees vs. Red Sox.
Though seeded as Wild Cards, New York and Boston are heavyweight entries in the 2026 postseason field. And only one can advance out of the best-of-three Wild Card Series that begins -- and takes place entirely -- in the Bronx on Tuesday.
The Yankees have survived most of the season without captain Aaron Judge, while the Red Sox survived a brutal start that had them 14 games under .500 in late June.
But who will survive this short and scintillating series at Yankee Stadium? Let’s break it down, position by position, and we are sure to find the unmistakably correct prediction, right? Right?!
Catcher
Austin Wells just hasn’t produced with the consistency he did in his Rookie of the Year finalist season in 2024 or the power he had in last year’s 20-homer, 20-double campaign. He’s a fantastic framer and blocker, and that could matter more in the postseason than his bat given the pitching staff’s increased importance in a short series. But Rutschman has those same strengths, along with an elite caught stealing track record, to go with higher offensive upside in a season in which he’s posted an above-average OPS+.
Edge: Red Sox
First base
The Red Sox have a major asset, but also a major question mark in Willson Contreras. He was a monumental offseason pickup in a trade with the Cardinals. The veteran produced his best offensive season yet, with an OPS over .900 and career-highs in homers and RBIs.
But when Contreras was plunked in the hand by a pitch late in the regular season, it complicated the equation. As of this writing, it was still not clear if he would suit up for the Wild Card Series. Even if he does, he might need some time to get back in the swing of things, given the impact hand discomfort can have on a power stroke.
So the Yankees’ successful midseason acquisition of Luis García Jr. looms large here. After an offensive breakthrough with the Nationals, he’s remained an above-average producer in pinstripes, finishing off his 30-homer season. And the Yanks have a dangerous platoon option in Paul Goldschmidt, the consummate pro who still does big damage to lefties – no small tool in their chest given the lefty leaning complexion of the Red Sox’s starting staff.
Edge: Yankees
Second base
Between the trade of the disappointing Marcelo Mayer and a late-season injury to Anthony Siegler, the Red Sox are left piecing things together here with Nick Sogard and veteran Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Sogard’s contact skills can play up in the postseason even if he doesn’t produce much power.
But the Yankees have higher upside here. Though Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s walk year saw statistical regression, he ultimately provided league-average offense with north of 40 steals. He could augment his open-market asking price with a strong showing.
Edge: Yankees
Shortstop
Trevor Story was sidelined for the Sox for about three months with a sports hernia that required surgery. He showed signs of offensive life in September, but this will nevertheless go down as one of his worst seasons at the plate in limited time.
The Yankees look like they have a star in the making in George Lombard Jr. While no one knows how the fresh-faced 21-year-old, who only debuted on Aug. 4, will perform under the bright lights of the postseason, he’s already had some huge hits for the Yanks and his plate discipline, high baseball IQ, fluid actions and plus speed all make him dangerous in a short series.
Edge: Yankees
Third base
The hot corner has been cold to the Yankees this year. Veteran Ryan McMahon’s first full season in the Bronx has been a drastic disappointment and his right-handed-hitting complement Amed Rosario hasn’t been much better. The Yankees were toying with the idea of working former shortstop Anthony Volpe here.
As for Boston, while replacing free-agent departure Alex Bregman was a tall order, a trade for Caleb Durbin, a reigning NL Rookie of the Year finalist with the Brewers, has paid enormous dividends. Durbin looked lost in the headlights for his first couple months in a major market, but his midseason ignition matched that of the club at large. He has great range at third, is among the more difficult batters in MLB to strike out and logged 25 doubles for the second straight season.
Edge: Red Sox
Left field
After getting spurned by Juan Soto in free agency the previous winter, the Yankees did not let Cody Bellinger get away. In his second season with the Yanks, the former NL MVP became an All-Star Game MVP in the midst of providing his usual disciplined, contact-and-power profile at the plate and elite defense in the grass. He’s been on this postseason stage plenty of times before.
There was hope in Boston that Roman Anthony would break out into superstardom this season. But a significant finger ligament injury early in the season got in the way, opening the door for Jarren Duran to see the bulk of time in left while producing an OPS+ more than 20% below league average. Anthony returned in late August, and it should shock no one if this postseason turns into his coming-out party. But for now, we’ve got to go with the more accomplished veteran here.
Edge: Yankees
Center field
The Sox had another late-season health scare with Ceddanne Rafaela, their rangy, speedy power-armed gem in center field. Rafaela was finishing up his finest offensive season to date when he suffered a right quad strain a few weeks back. But a clean MRI in the season’s final week allowed him to return.
Meanwhile, Trent Grisham’s September hamstring strain gave the Yankees their own center-field concern. Grisham’s absence allowed 25-year-old rookie Spencer Jones to showcase his excellent raw power and athleticism. Grisham could be back for this series. But Rafaela’s offensive breakthrough and Gold Glove defense carry the way here.
Edge: Red Sox
Right field
Judge’s calf injury is probably the biggest X-factor in the entire postseason field. The Yankees were cagey about its severity, and manager Aaron Boone said the club was preparing for a Wild Card Series without the captain. Judge was intent on trying to make his way back. But ultimately, Judge was left off the Bombers' Wild Card roster, so they'll be down one of the best hitters on the planet.
For the Red Sox, Wilyer Abreu is ready for his close-up. He was a durable doubles machine who also reached career highs in homers and RBIs, he dramatically improved his production against left-handed pitching, and he has range and a mammoth arm in right. His surge was essential in the Sox returning to the postseason.
Edge: Red Sox
Designated hitter
With Masataka Yoshida out with a hamstring strain, Boston will utilize a DH platoon that includes Roman Anthony against righties and Jahmai Jones against lefties.
In a season that has included so little Judge, the Yankees have gotten a ton out of Ben Rice. Last season’s surprise ascendence for the New England native has proven to be only an appetizer. Rice showed he can mash both lefties and righties alike in clearing the 40-homer threshold, getting selected as a first-time All-Star and earning down-ballot MVP support.
Edge: Yankees
Starting pitching
Cam Schlittler’s likely Cy Young-winning breakthrough in 2026 came on the heels of him carving up the Red Sox club he grew up rooting for in last year’s Wild Card Series. He pairs with Max Fried and Gerrit Cole to give the Yankees a terrifying top end of the rotation in this short series, even if the finish on Cole’s pitches is not yet what it was prior to Tommy John.
While the Yankees deserve the edge here, that’s not to suggest the Sox are slouches in the starting department. That they got to this point essentially without Garrett Crochet took a lot of fortitude, and Payton Tolle’s fantastic rookie campaign was one of the most fun storylines of the season. Sonny Gray remains an absolute command artist in his age-36 season, and Ranger Suarez was a terrific offseason signing who drastically limits the kind of hard contact that can change games in October.
Still, it’s the Yanks here.
Edge: Yankees
Bullpen
These are two top-five relief units in terms of both ERA and expected ERA. Both are excellent at suppressing long balls, which is crucial in October.
The Yankees have a strong ninth-inning anchor in David Bednar, whose elite ability to generate chase with his four-steam/split/curve mix can neutralize even the biggest bats. Paul Blackburn has gone from oft-injured starter to absolute force of nature in the setup role, and Brent Headrick has also undergone a massive transformation as a member of the Yankees ‘pen, for whom he has emerged as a whiff machine. The strength of the starting staff has trickled down to a Yankees bullpen that ranks among the lowest innings workloads of any relief unit in MLB this season.
With Tyron Guerrero’s recent return from injury and the presence of Garrett Whitlock, Greg Weissert and lefty Jovani Morán, the Sox are well-situated in their bridge to the ninth. And in the ninth, they’ve got the ageless Aroldis Chapman, whose age-38 season has seen him produce yet another sub-2.00 ERA, another ERA+ more than 100% better than league average and upper-echelon velo and strikeout rates. He recently returned from a late-season lat issue. Between Chapman’s presence and the possibility that Crochet’s elite arsenal impacts the ‘pen in his potential return from injury, the Red Sox earn the edge.
Edge: Red Sox
Prediction
The Yankees were the better team in record and run differential, and they did it mostly without Judge. They hold the home-field and rotation advantages, have a higher run-scoring baseline and are, therefore, the clear favorites.
All reasons why I’m taking the Red Sox in three. Because baseball.

item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.

The 2026 Major League Baseball season has been anything but smooth for Boston Red Sox outfielder Jarren Duran, but he still has found a way to put himself into some elite company.
Duran has taken a lot of heat all season to this point. He's batting .207 this season and striking out a lot and not walking much. In fact, Duran's 39 walks this season are his fewest since 2023. That year, he only played 102 games. This season, he has 147 games under his belt. He hasn't gotten on base a lot, but the power numbers have still been there. Duran has 20 homers on the season, which is one off from his career high of 21, which he set in his All-Star season in 2024. He has driven in 69 runs this year. Plus, despite the fact that he hasn't been on base much, he has still been a terror on the basepaths. On Wednesday, he recorded his 20th stolen base of the season.
Now, Duran has two 20-20 seasons under his belt and is just the third member of the organization, along with Mookie Betts and Jackie Jensen, to record multiple, per former Red Sox director of baseball communications and media relations JP Long.
"Jarren Duran (2024, ’26) joins Mookie Betts (2016, ’17, ’18) and Jackie Jensen (1954, ’59) as the only Red Sox to record multiple 20-HR/20-SB seasons," Long wrote. "Jarren and Mookie are the only Red Sox ever to record 3 consecutive seasons of at least 15 HR and 20 steals."
Who Saw That Coming?
Talk about improbable, huh?
The last time Duran had a 20-20 season, he was a 9.0-WAR player and finished the season with 21 homers, 75 RBIs, 34 stolen bases, 48 doubles, 14 triples and a .285/.342/.492 slash line. He was incredible and led the league in both doubles and triples.
The 2026 season hasn't been kind to him, but quietly he has still had an impact. He's slashing .207/.265/.364. If you look around the league and see numbers like those, you're not going to typically see 20 homers and 20 stolen bases as well. That doesn't make the .207 batting average any better, but it is a bit of a silver lining in an otherwise difficult season. The talent is there. There's no denying that. Boston has to find a way to get him back to the 2024 version of himself. But for now, this is something to celebrate.

Across 182 innings (31 starts) in 2026, Seattle Mariners starting pitcher Logan Gilbert has recorded a 12-11 record with a 3.81 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 197 strikeouts. After posting a 32.3% strikeout rate in 2025, Gilbert's strikeout rate has fallen to 26.7% in 2026. The 29-year-old's numbers have taken a considerable hit lately, as he's posted a 6.65 ERA across 21 2/3 innings in September. Surrendering the long ball has been a major issue for Gilbert in the second half of the season. Across 56 1/3 innings (10 starts) since the beginning of August, Gilbert has allowed 14 home runs (2.20 HR/9). Heading into his final scheduled start of 2026 against the Los Angeles Angels on Sunday, fantasy managers may want to temper expectations for the usually dependable Gilbert.--Will Brady

Brown has had issues with command all year long, and his 11.9% walk rate has led to an elevated WHIP. Heading into his final start of the regular season on Saturday against the Athletics, Brown is beginning to look like the fantasy ace he was drafted to be ahead of 2026.--Will Brady

item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA) finished his marvelous regular season with another strong performance, firing six shutout innings on 77 pitches, allowing four hits and one walk while striking out three. Next start? Game 1 or 2 of next week’s AL Wild Card Series, all but certain to be at Yankee Stadium.
“He looked fantastic,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “Had his spin. Was in the zone. Was ahead in the count. He looked really good. It was good to see.”
Even better to see was the return of All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman, who hadn’t pitched since Sept. 13 because of a lat issue. All the 38-year-old did was overpower the Guardians by striking out the side (all swinging) in order on 12 pitches. That’s all it took for career save No. 402 and 35th this season.
“I felt good and happy to be able to go out there,” said Chapman. “I felt like my pitches and my stuff were very good today. So I’m happy to be back. I feel normal. I feel like I’m at 100 percent right now.”
That is certainly good news for the Red Sox, who need their closer in top form to make a deep postseason run.
“He looked sharp,” said Tracy. “That was also really good to see.”
For the first time in weeks, Tracy was able to deploy his 7-8-9 relief crew in Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock and Chapman. All three relievers had injuries at various times down the stretch but are trending well now.
“That was great,” said Tracy. “To be perfectly honest with you, that was kind of planned out regardless of how the game went. So to be able to score a run prior to that section of relievers coming in was fantastic.”
And while hits with runners in scoring position (2-for-14, 11 left on base) were again a rare commodity for Boston, Andruw Monasterio broke out of an 0-for-21 slump by belting an RBI single with two outs in the sixth that scored Jarren Duran from second.
In a game in which neither team had an extra-base hit, combining instead for 17 singles, Monasterio’s knock was the difference in the ballgame.
“I was fighting myself just yesterday and tonight about my approach,” said Monasterio. “I just had to get through it. And I did it.”
In this final homestand of the regular season, the main focus for the Red Sox is having their house in order for what’s to come next week.
There was some cause for concern in that regard, as center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, after his first at-bat back from a three-week absence with a right quadriceps strain, had to exit in the top of the third with right hamstring tightness.
The Red Sox are hopeful it was a mild setback.
“I think it was just a cramp,” said Rafaela. “Maybe not hydrated enough. And I got that cramp right there and just didn't want to risk going for the double. And then, obviously, it’s Trace just trying to protect me, with big things in front of us. And so I think it's just that.”

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox pulled off a 1-0 series-evening win over the visiting Cleveland Guardians on Wednesday night, despite the ongoing dearth of situational hitting that has plagued them for the last two weeks and intermittently throughout the season.
Boston batters tallied 12 hits, but went 2 for 14 with runners in scoring position, and left 11 men on base in eight innings.
Fortunately for the home team, Sonny Gray was on form in his final start of the regular season. The veteran right-hander tossed six shutout innings, with four hits, one walk and three strikeouts.
Gray’s sixth scoreless start of at least six innings this year tied his single-season high first set in 2015 and matched in 2025. He is the first Red Sox pitcher to make at least six such starts in his age-36 season or older since Luis Tiant in 1977, and only the fourth in franchise history (also Cy Young, Lefty Grove).
“Just a really good pitcher,” manager Chad Tracy said of his starter. “The level of consistency for him from start to finish has been very fun to watch, and impressive.”
Though Gray’s pitch count sat at 77 (52 for strikes) after the sixth and the game remained scoreless, Tracy went to his bullpen. With Boston’s postseason ticket punched on Sunday, the short hook could suggest Gray is getting the ball for Game 1 of the Wild Card series on Tuesday.
Cleveland southpaw Foster Griffin was not nearly as adept at keeping the Red Sox off the diamond. He struck out seven and issued no walks, but yielded 10 hits in six innings of one-run ball.
Save for Jarren Duran’s leadoff single and Andruw Monasterio’s two-out RBI single in the sixth, the Red Sox bailed Griffin out every time. They were 2 for 11 RISP through his six innings. Their nine men left on base during Griffin’s start included multiple in four of the first five frames and bases-loaded in the third.
“Yeah, I mean, take the positives,” Tracy said of the offense. “I thought we swung the bat great. We actually got some hits today. … Between (the two-out hits) and the accumulation of hits and base runners throughout the game, I thought it was a pretty good offensive night. Obviously you’d like to score more, but we did take better plate appearances.”
Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman, Boston’s elite bullpen trio all season long, ensured the slim lead held until the end with a scoreless inning apiece. Tracy revealed postgame their appearances were “planned out, regardless of how the game went.”
“That was great,” Tracy said. “To be able to score a run prior to that section of relievers coming in was fantastic.”
Duran, who replaced Ceddanne Rafaela in center field in the top of the third, led off the bottom of the eighth with a single. His subsequent steal of second made 2026 his second career season with 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases (also 2024). Duran, Mookie Betts and Jackie Jensen are the only players in franchise history with multiple 20-20 seasons.
Rafaela’s first game back from a 10-day stint on the injured list with a right quad strain began in energetic fashion. He recorded each of the first three outs, including a diving catch to rob Guardians hitter Steven Kwan of a leadoff single.
But after pulling up lame at first base on his own leadoff single in the bottom of the second, Rafaela ultimately left the game with right hamstring tightness when the inning turned over. Tracy announced postgame that Rafaela will undergo an MRI on Thursday.
“No, I think it’s more frustrating (than disappointing),” Tracy said of the Rafaela situation. “You want to see everybody get to that finish line healthy.
“So more just when you see it, you’re concerned, you know? So (we) don’t know where we’re at with it yet. Hopefully, it’s not a huge deal, but still, yeah, makes your heart jump a little bit, and we’ll see where he’s at.”
Cleveland threatened against Whitlock in an eighth inning that saw both teams run out of ABS challenges. No. 9 hitter Brayan Rocchio led off with a single, and Whitlock issued a one-out walk to third baseman José Ramírez before getting an inning-ending double play from designated hitter Chase DeLauter.
After the Red Sox stranded Duran in the bottom of the eighth, Chapman took the mound for the first time since Sept. 13. Boston’s All-Star closer was back in top form after being day-to-day with lat tightness. He struck out the side, Jo Adell, and pinch-hitters Angel Martínez and Angel Genao on 12 pitches.
The Red Sox are 85-73 with four games left to play. Wednesday marked Tracy’s first win since the interim tag was removed on Tuesday.

The 30-year-old outfielder stole his 20th base of the season on Wednesday night, joining an exclusive club in team history.
BOSTON -- The Boston Red Sox beat the Cleveland Guardians 1-0 on Wednesday night to improve to 85-73 and set up a rubber match on Thursday night. It was supposed to be a night off for struggling outfielder Jarren Duran, however, after center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela exited the game in the third inning with a right hamstring injury, the 30-year-old Duran was thrust into action, joining an exclusive list in the franchise's 125-year history in the process.
Duran's first at-bat in the third inning ended in disappointment as he struck out with the bases loaded to end the scoring chance for Boston. However, the 30-year-old turned in a strong performance in relief of the injured Rafaela, leading off the bottom of the sixth inning with a single, later coming around to score the game's lone run on a single off the bat of second baseman Andruw Monasterio.
Duran again reached base leading off the eighth inning with a sharply hit line drive to right field. With Boston leading 1-0, the speedster did everything he could to get the team in a position to add on. With third baseman Caleb Durbin at the plate, Duran took off for second base, diving in safely for his 20th stolen base of the year, securing the second 20-home-run, 20-steal season of his career.
Duran became just the third player in Red Sox history to post multiple 20/20 seasons, joining 2018 Most Valuable Player Mookie Betts, who did so three times during his six-year tenure in Boston, and Jackie Jensen, who accomplished the feat twice.
Reaching 20 home runs and 20 steals is an impressive accomplishment for Duran in an otherwise unimpressive season. The 30-year-old has been one of baseball's most disappointing players in 2026, hitting just .207/.265/.364/.629 in 147 games. The 30-year-old ranks in the bottom five among 133 qualified hitters in batting average (129th), on-base percentage (133rd), and OPS (131st).
Despite those struggles, Duran has still found a way to provide some value to the team in both the power and speed departments.
In other Red Sox news
Manager Chad Tracy told reporters, including Tim Healey of the Boston Globe, that Rafaela will undergo an MRI on his right hamstring. Rafaela described the injury as "cramping" that he felt on a swing, rather than when he ran to first base on his second-inning single.
As reported by MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo, 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet is scheduled to throw another live bullpen session this weekend as he tries to return from left shoulder inflammation and join the Red Sox in a bullpen role for the postseason. Crochet will not make a regular-season appearance before potentially joining the active roster for the Wild Card round.
With a nor'easter expected to hit New England beginning Friday night, Major League Baseball has moved the Red Sox regular-season finale to Friday afternoon as part of a day-night doubleheader, starting at 1:05 p.m. ET. The league also moved up the start time for Friday's regularly scheduled game from 7:10 p.m. ET to 6:05 p.m. ET. As of now, no changes have been made to Saturday's game.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to win the series from the Guardians in Thursday night's rubber match at Fenway Park. Ranger Suarez (8-4, 3.27 ERA) will make his final regular-season start for Boston, while Cleveland has not yet named its starter. First pitch is set for 6:45 p.m. ET.

Andruw Monasterio’s sixth-inning RBI single and Sonny Gray’s six shutout innings propelled the Boston Red Sox to a 1-0 win over the visiting Cleveland Guardians on Wednesday night.
The Red Sox (85-73) managed the lone run on 12 hits, all singles. They went 1-for-9 with runners in scoring position and left eight men on base through five innings before Monasterio’s run-scoring, two-out knock off Cleveland starter Foster Griffin (15-6) broke the deadlock.
In the sixth, Jarren Duran (2-for-3) lined a leadoff single to left and moved to second on a groundout. He scored from second base on Monasterio’s knock, sliding ahead of left fielder Steven Kwan’s relay throw and catcher Patrick Bailey’s tag.
Gray (18-5) struck out three while allowing four hits and one walk to increase his American League-leading win total. Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman each threw a scoreless inning to finish off Boston’s 17th shutout victory of the season.
Chapman struck out the side in the ninth to log his 35th save as Boston snapped a three-game losing streak.
Red Sox center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela returned from a 17-game injury absence caused by a right quad strain to record all three outs in the first, including a spectacular diving catch on Kwan, the leadoff hitter who still went 2-for-4 for Cleveland (82-76).
Griffin worked six frames, striking out seven and allowing one run on 10 hits and no walks.
The Guardians remained one game up on the White Sox (81-77) in the American League Central after Chicago lost 5-4 at Kansas City on Wednesday.
Rafaela hit a leadoff single in the second inning but appeared to be in pain after reaching first. He stayed in the game to run the bases and initially took his defensive position before Duran replaced him. The Red Sox announced that Rafaela was dealing with right hamstring tightness.
Rafaela’s defense helped Gray retire the first six men he faced. Bailey recorded Cleveland’s first hit with a leadoff single in the third, but a 6-3 double play ended the inning without any damage. Gray fanned a pair of Guardians to strand two to end the fourth.
After the lone run scored and Gray exited, Guerrero struck out three in the seventh after a leadoff walk. Whitlock worked around Brayan Rocchio’s leadoff single and Jose Ramirez’s one-out walk in the eighth, inducing an inning-ending double-play grounder from Chase DeLauter.

item.content:encoded:
Ceddanne Rafaela’s first game back from the 10-day injured list (right quad strain) lasted all of two innings before the Red Sox removed him for seemingly precautionary reasons.
Boston’s Gold Glove center fielder caught all three outs in the top of the first, even laying out for a diving catch of Cleveland Guardians’ Steven Kwan’s leadoff line drive.
But when Rafaela singled to lead off the bottom of the second, he grimaced as he ran and seemed to pull up lame on first base. He leaned over briefly as he stood on the bag, prompting a visit from manager Chad Tracy and a team trainer. After a few minutes’ discussion and some test running down the first base line, they allowed Rafaela to remain in the game.
Rafaela appeared to run normally as he advanced to second when Caleb Durbin reached first on a fielding error by third baseman José Ramírez, and initially remained on the field after the Red Sox failed to score in the bottom of the second. But Jarren Duran replaced him in center before the top of the third began.
“Just saw him continuing to flex it,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy told ESPN’s Buster Olney moments later on the game broadcast. “That’s all. He seemed to have felt some cramping in the back there. When he went back out there, he kept flexing it, so we said, let’s go ahead and make the change.”
Red Sox media relations announced Rafaela left the game with “right hamstring tightness” two innings later.
The Red Sox already planned to monitor Rafaela’s workload in Wednesday’s game, as the end of the Triple-A season on Sunday meant he returned without playing in single a rehab game.
“You guys know, every ball that gets hit up in the air in his direction, he thinks he can catch it,” Tracy said pregame. “So if you have a very normal, easy game flow, I think he’d be just fine. If you have a game flow where he tracks down seven balls in the gap and hits two doubles, you might say that’s enough.
“We’ll be very reactive to what the game is requiring of him and do our best to make sure we keep him in a good spot.”
Rafaela’s departure had consequences for the Red Sox almost immediately. They loaded the bases in the bottom of the third on back-to-back singles by Roman Anthony and Nick Sogard, and a two-out single by Adley Rutschman. Duran, batting in Rafaela’s No. 6 spot in the order, struck out swinging to end the inning.

The Boston Red Sox kept outfielder Jarren Duran out of the starting lineup again Wednesday night as they hosted the Cleveland Guardians in the second game of a three-game series at Fenway Park.
Manager Chad Tracy’s posted batting order featured Roman Anthony in left field, Nick Sogard at first base, Jahmai Jones as the designated hitter, Wilyer Abreu in right field, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Ceddanne Rafaela in center field, Caleb Durbin at third base, Trevor Story at shortstop and Andruw Monasterio at second base. Sonny Gray was listed as the starting pitcher.
Duran also sat Tuesday, when the Guardians beat the Red Sox 3-2. He entered that game as a pinch-hitter and drew a walk.
Cleveland took the series opener on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly in the ninth inning. The Guardians stranded 15 runners but still extended their winning streak to six games.
Boston dropped to 84-73. The club already clinched an American League Wild Card berth Sunday but has lost three straight and eight of its last 12.
Duran entered Wednesday batting .204 with 110 hits, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 65 runs and 19 stolen bases in 146 games. He had 538 at-bats, 39 walks and 163 strikeouts.
The left-handed hitter has struggled in September. He was 9-for-50 with one home run and one RBI in 17 games this month before Tuesday’s appearance.
Over his last 15 games he was 8-for-42 with one homer. His on-base-plus-slugging percentage sat at .625 for the season.
Rafaela’s return to center field tightened the outfield picture. Anthony has been starting in left and Abreu in right, leaving Duran as the extra outfielder in many recent games.
Tracy had the interim tag removed Tuesday and was named the franchise’s 49th manager. The Red Sox have used a mix of platoons and rest days for Duran down the stretch.
Gray brings a 17-5 record and 2.82 ERA into the start. Cleveland is expected to counter with Forrest Griffin.
The Guardians sit at 82-75 and hold a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox in the AL Central. Chicago owns the season-series tiebreaker.
Duran, 30, is in his sixth major league season, all with Boston. He was an All-Star in 2024.
He still ranks among the team leaders in home runs and RBIs despite the low batting average. His 20 homers leave him one short of his career high.
The Red Sox close the regular season with this series, then host the Chicago Cubs for three games. Seeding and rest for the Wild Card round remain in play.
Duran’s speed and defense have kept him in the mix even as his batting average dropped. He stole 19 bases and continued to play a plus outfield when used.
Boston’s offense produced eight hits Tuesday. Rutschman went 3-for-4 and pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper tied the game with a home run in the eighth.
Cleveland collected 12 hits. Angel Martínez finished 3-for-4.
The Red Sox sit 12 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East. The Yankees hold the other Wild Card spot six games ahead of Boston.
Duran’s role for the final week and any postseason series will depend on how Tracy balances the four outfielders available.

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses whether or not the Red Sox have enough offensive firepower to win a World Series on the 'Bleav in Boston' podcast. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
The Boston Red Sox have a well-documented outfield logjam, with Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, and Roman Anthony. But could the team be preparing to add another piece to the already confusing puzzle? At least one person thinks so, as Seattle Mariners beat reporter Ryan Divish linked pending free-agent Randy Arozarena to Boston in an appearance on the 'Foul Territory' podcast.
What did Divish say?
"They're [Seattle] going to lose their best player. Randy Arozarena is going to be a free agent. I think we all know Randy would probably prefer to stay on the East Coast," Divish said. "I'm guessing Boston is ready to cut a huge check for him," he continued.
Is Arozarena a fit?
From a sheer production perspective, the 31-year-old could be the missing piece for a Red Sox offense that still feels a bat short. Arozarena is coming off the best two seasons of his career, hitting .258/.355/.453/.808 with 53 home runs, 63 doubles, and 152 RBI en route to back-to-back All-Star selections, all while playing half of his games in one of the most pitcher-friendly environments in the sport, Seattle's T-Mobile Park.
Arozarena has also had incredible success at Fenway Park, posting a .278/.351/.481/.833 slash line with five home runs, 12 doubles, and 19 RBI in career 32 games. He also fits the profile of hitters that Boston has targeted under Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, pulling the ball in the air at a consistent rate. Along with a strong track record at Fenway Park, Arozarena has proven himself in the postseason, hitting .292/.380/.565/.946 in 45 playoff games, including being named ALCS Most Valuable Player in 2020 with the Tampa Bay Rays.
However, bringing in the veteran outfielder would require significant roster reshuffling, including moving both an outfielder and the designated hitter, Masataka Yoshida.
Our take
If Arozarena is set on returning to the East Coast, he could be the perfect fit for the Red Sox offense. His defensive metrics at this stage of his career suggest he's best suited as a designated hitter, and the Red Sox have gotten some of the worst production in baseball from their revolving door of designated hitters in 2026. He also has a proven track record of success at both Fenway Park and in the postseason.
While signing him would require some roster maneuvering, including potentially selling Duran at his lowest possible value or eating the $18.6 million remaining on Masataka Yoshida's contract, Arozarena is about as perfect fit as you can get for the Red Sox in what's set to be a weak class of free-agent bats, especially if the offense comes up short in the playoffs for the second consecutive season.
Up next for the Sox
After clinching a playoff berth on Sunday afternoon, the Red Sox are off on Monday before opening up the final homestand of the regular season on Tuesday, welcoming the Cleveland Guardians to Fenway Park for a three-game set. Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02 ERA) will get the start opposite fellow rookie left-hander Parker Messick (12-9, 2.57 ERA) for Cleveland. First pitch is set for 6:45 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ odds of winning the AL East are down to 2.8 percent per FanGraphs after getting walked off by the Diamondbacks last night. I know mathematically that makes sense, but the chances mentally feel even more extreme. I’ve been having “fun” (or whatever) comping the odds to certain pitchers from history getting a hit. We are the dregs. Remember mid-2000s Mets pitcher Aaron Heilman? I personally remember him most for giving up the homer to Yadier Molina late in Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS, just before Adam Wainwright famously caught Carlos Beltrán looking to win the pennant.
Anyway, Heilman was a horrendous hitter. He singled once in his rookie year, and then never got another hit. He ended his career 1-for-47, so an .021 average. So the Yankees just need magic only a little bit more sufficient than that RBI single by Heilman off Sidney Ponson on August 12, 2003! Hell yeah.
It’s not happening, but we press on because it’s good to check up on what everyone else is doing anyway. Here’s what was going on Saturday.
Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) 2, Boston Red Sox (84-71) 1
The Yankees gained a full game on the Rays on Friday for the first time in over a week, as Boston snapped their six-game winning streak. There was no such fortune to be found yesterday though; Tampa Bay made sure of that well before first pitch in Arizona, and it only got worse from there. By the end of the night, the Rays once again had a five-game lead over the Yanks; Tampa Bay’s magic number (combination of Rays wins or Yankees losses) to clinch the AL East is four.
This one was a pitchers’ duel to the bitter end. Brayan Bello had easily his best outing of a turbulent season (and probably the best of his career), firing eight shutout frames at the Trop and fanning 11 Rays, tying a personal best from July 9, 2024. As he only went 5.1 in that one and faced merely the soon-to-depart-Oakland A’s rather than the division-leading Rays.
The only true blemish on Bello’s record came when Jonathan Aranda cracked an opposite-field homer to make it a 1-1 game in the fourth. Tampa Bay had a chance to make it 2-1 against Bello in the seventh when Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson led off with singles. Bello then induced a grounder from Victor Mesa Jr. to move up the runners, and then another off the bat of Richie Palacios to Trevor Story, who nailed pinch-runner Jonny DeLuca at home. Palacios swiped second, but Bello fanned Cedric Mullins to end the inning. The Rays went down in order in the eighth to end Bello’s brilliant night.
Unfortunately for Bello, a win wasn’t in the cards because Boston put up next to nothing against Freddy Peralta and the Rays’ pitching staff. Doubles by Caleb Durbin and Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox their one run in the second, but they were stymied from there. They had chances!
- Second inning after Anthony’s two-out double: Mickey Gasper lineout to center
- Fourth inning with runners on first and second, one out: Story strikeout, Durbin popout
- Fifth inning with runner on second, one out: Anthony groundout, Gasper strikeout
- Sixth inning with runners on first and second, two out: Durbin fly out to left
- Eighth inning after Adley Rutschman’s one-out double: Wilyer Abreu strikeout, Nick Sogard lineout
Even against lockdown Rays closer Bryan Baker, Boston had one last shot to take a late lead. After Story grounded out, Durbin lined a double down the left field line to put himself in scoring position for Jarren Duran. Durbin darted from second, however, and got thrown out stealing third. Duran promptly followed with a triple over DeLuca’s head in center. Isiah Kiner-Falefa bounced one to Junior Caminero at third to end the threat.
Granted a chance to walk it off, Tampa Bay didn’t waste it. Rather than blasting a homer to finish the game as he had twice earlier this homestand, Caminero began the ninth against Garrett Whitlock with a single to left. (A catwalk curtailed Durbin’s effort to catch a popup earlier in the AB.) DeLuca popped up, but Chandler Simpson grounded one through the six-hole for another hit. The runners moved up when catcher Connor Wong let a Whitlock sinker up bounce off his glove for a passed ball. Palacios ended the night with flare to center that fell in, securing the win for Tampa Bay. At least the Wild Card Series is also almost certainly going to be at Yankee Stadium now, I suppose.
AL Rock Fight
Cleveland Guardians (80-75) 12, The Athletics (61-94) 6
Two crooked numbers effectively decided Saturday’s affair with the A’s in a hurry. Tanner Bibee kind of stunk and would allow six runs in a dozen hits while failing to make through five, but it hardly mattered. Cleveland erased a 2-0 deficit in the first on a three-run shot from rookie Chase DeLauter and two-run homer by Angel Martinez. The A’s got one back in the third, only to see another five-spot from the Guardians on poor Jacob Lopez as David Fry, Austin Hedges, and Brayan Rocchio all delivered RBI doubles. Martinez later added a homer and an RBI single in a career-best four-hit day.
Chicago White Sox (79-76) 3, Detroit Tigers (73-82) 1
Cleveland’s win meant that Chicago was stuck at a game back in the AL Central in the best-case, but they did at least help push one of their Wild Card foes out of the picture with a win. Honestly, this was probably kind of a dud of a game for anyone who isn’t a White Sox fan, the lone highlights being Sean Burke’s six scoreless frames and Miguel Vargas’ sixth-inning solo shot to make it 3-1, Chicago (the other runs scored on an RBI single by Munetaka Murakami and a fifth-inning sac fly). Spencer Torkelson had a chance to tie the game with a homer following Hao-Yu Lee’s two-out single in the ninth, but he flew out to center to end it.
Milwaukee Brewers (97-58) 1, Baltimore Orioles (75-80) 0
Yeah, it’s time to stick a fork in the O’s. It was all but certain for awhile now, but Chicago’s win combined with Baltimore’s second-straight loss to Milwaukee means that the Orioles are four back with a week to play, plus multiple teams in front of them. Trevor Rogers was the hard-luck loser here while Baltimore got blanked on four hits and Rece Hinds lost a fly ball from Joey Ortiz in the sun, allowing him to triple and score on Gary Sánchez’s RBI grounder. Woof.
Texas Rangers (78-77) 6, Toronto Blue Jays (76-79) 1
The O’s aren’t the only bird that are all but shot down, either. Trade Deadline acquisition José Soriano coughed up an early homer to Josh Jung, beginning a five-inning, six-run outing that pushed Toronto three games out in the Wild Card and the Rangers into a one-game AL West lead over Houston. The only downside for Texas was that second-half surprise Cal Quantrill—who has a 1.75 ERA since re-entering the rotation in late July—left in the second with lat tightness, so old friend Jordan Montgomery picked up the slack in long relief, retiring 11 of the 12 hitters he faced with no hits allowed.
Atlanta Braves (91-64) 6, Houston Astros (77-78) 3
Houston and Texas have been wrestling all week over the prestigious “Who can win this horri-awful division with a .500-ish record” crown. Sunday it went to Texas with the Astros falling out of their tie for first place (remember that they own the tiebreaker). Isaac Paredes had put Houston ahead with a solo homer and an RBI knock in the third, but the Astros’ bullpen set that lead on fire. The big blow came off the bat of Ronald Acuña Jr., who belted a grand slam off Bryan Abreu in the seventh after AJ Blubaugh made a right mess of things.

The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adjustment involving outfielder Jarren Duran, via Underdog MLB.
After sitting out the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Duran will slide up one spot into the seventh hole. He will hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton while remaining in center field, the position he has occupied since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White opened the job.
The rest of the order features Roman Anthony in left, Mickey Gasper at designated hitter, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Trevor Story at shortstop, Nick Sogard at first, and Cooper Durbin at third.
The move comes during a difficult individual season for Duran. Entering Sunday he is hitting .206 in 144 games, with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs and 69 RBIs. His slugging percentage sits at .364 and his OPS at .626.
Speculation about a possible trade lingered for weeks before the August 4 deadline, yet Duran remained in a Red Sox uniform and has continued to receive regular playing time as the club pushes toward October.
Boston sits at 84-71 with seven games left and occupies what currently looks like the second American League Wild Card spot. Should the standings hold, the Red Sox would open the postseason on the road in a best-of-three Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
Every remaining game, including Sunday’s finale against a familiar division rival, therefore carries playoff implications.
Tracy’s decision to bump Duran up in the order is a small tactical shift rather than a wholesale overhaul, but it signals a willingness to tinker as the club tries to generate more consistent offense down the stretch.
Whether the extra spot in the lineup produces results remains to be seen.
Duran’s season-long struggles have been well documented, yet he has shown flashes of the power and speed that once made him a fixture in the middle of Boston’s order.
A productive afternoon against Jax and the Rays would give the Red Sox a series victory and a bit of momentum heading into the final week.
With the calendar now late September and the postseason picture still taking shape, even incremental lineup changes can feel significant.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Richie Palacios dropped a blooper into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give the Tampa Bay Rays a 2-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Saturday.
Tampa Bay, which has three walk-off wins on its current homestand, lowered its magic number to clinch the AL East to five games. The second-place Yankees are in Arizona on Saturday night.
Prior to Palacios’ single, the Rays were 0 for 17 with runners in scoring position over the first two games of the series. The postseason-bound Rays, who’ve won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth.
First, Caminero’s foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong’s passed ball moved Caminero to third.
Bidding to clinch a wild-card berth, the Red Sox squandered a prime opportunity in the top of the ninth.
Facing closer Bryan Baker (4-2) in a tie game, Boston got a double from Caleb Durbin and a triple from Jarren Duran. However, Nick Fortes threw out Durbin stealing third before Duran’s triple, and Caminero made a stellar play at third base to retire Isiah Kiner-Falefa, stranding Duran.
Boston also wasted a phenomenal effort from starter Brayan Bello, who matched a career high with 11 strikeouts. In eight innings, he allowed five hits, one run and no walks. Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) was unavailable.
The Red Sox took a 1-0 lead with doubles from Durbin and Roman Anthony in the third inning. Trevor Story extended his hitting streak to 10 games with a sixth-inning single.
Jonathan Aranda tied it with an opposite-field solo homer on the first pitch of the Rays’ fourth.
The Rays are an MLB-best 25-14 in one-run games.
Boston could have clinched a playoff berth with a win combined with a loss by either the Rangers or Astros. Both of those teams were seven games behind the Red Sox with eight games remaining entering Saturday.
UP NEXT
Right-hander Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) gets the nod for the Rays on Sunday in the series finale. Boston had not announced a starter.

Caleb Durbin stroked two doubles and scored for the Red Sox (84-71), who lost for the first time in three games.
Starting pitcher Brayan Bello went a season-best eight innings and allowed one run on five hits with a career high-tying 11 strikeouts.
The Rays got an out with the infield drawn in and appeared to escape trouble in the third. Then Roman Anthony, who homered and had three RBIs in Friday's 4-2 win in the opener, remained hot and made it 1-0 with a two-out double that scored Durbin.
Cedric Mullins laid down a bunt single and reached second on Durbin's throwing error to open the third, but he was picked off and caught trying to steal third on Jorge Mateo's failed sacrifice bunt.
In the fourth, Aranda tied it 1-all when he rocked his 22nd homer to left field as he took Bello's 97 m.p.h. four-seam fastball the opposite way.
With Bello still in the game in the seventh, Hicks led off with a single and Simpson dropped one into right with no outs. Following a groundout and a fielder's choice, Bello ended the threat by whiffing Mullins on a foul tip.
